details:
**Leviathan**
Hobbes's 1651 masterpiece of political philosophy and the universal giveaway. Named after a sea monster from the Book of Job, it argues that people should submit to an all-powerful sovereign to escape the chaos of the state of nature, and its famous frontispiece shows a giant crowned figure made up of many tiny people.

**"Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short"**
Hobbes's description of human life in the state of nature, from chapter 13 of Leviathan. In this condition there is "no culture of the earth," "no commodious building," no arts, no letters, and no industry, because no one can trust that they will enjoy the fruits of their labor.

**"War of all against all" (bellum omnium contra omnes)**
Hobbes's term for the state of nature, a condition of perpetual war in which every person is an enemy to every other. He names competition, diffidence (distrust), and glory as the three principal causes of quarrel among men.

**Social contract and absolute sovereign**
Hobbes argued that people escape the state of nature by agreeing, through a covenant, to transfer their rights to a sovereign with absolute and indivisible power, a theory influenced by Jean Bodin. Subjects owe obedience as long as the sovereign protects them, since the right to self-preservation can never be given up.

**Natural equality: the ability to kill**
Hobbes argued that humans are roughly equal in body and mind, because even the weakest person can kill the strongest through cunning or by joining with others. This equality creates mutual fear and drives the war of all against all.

**"Kingdom of Darkness" and the "Confederacy of Deceivers"**
The title of Part IV of Leviathan, which attacks those who misinterpret Scripture to gain power, especially the Catholic Church. Hobbes describes the Kingdom of Darkness as a "confederacy of deceivers" and compares the papacy to a "kingdom of fairies," with the Pope as the ghost of the dead Roman Empire.

**"Of Man" and the opening chapters of Leviathan**
Part I of Leviathan builds Hobbes's political theory from definitions about human nature. He defines imagination as "nothing but decaying sense," describes passions as the interior beginnings of voluntary motions, and rejects any summum bonum (greatest good) in favor of continual desire.

**Three types of commonwealth**
In Leviathan, Hobbes recognizes only three forms of commonwealth based on who holds sovereignty: monarchy (one), aristocracy (an assembly of some), and democracy (an assembly of all). He considered monarchy the best.

**Justice as keeping covenants**
Hobbes's third law of nature is that men perform their covenants. He defines injustice as nothing other than the failure to perform a covenant, so that whatever is not unjust is just; before covenants and a sovereign exist, there is no justice or injustice.

**De Cive (On the Citizen)**
Hobbes's 1642 Latin treatise that first set out the political arguments he later expanded in Leviathan. It forms the third part of his Elements of Philosophy trilogy.

**De Corpore and De Homine (Elements of Philosophy)**
Hobbes's philosophical trilogy consists of De Corpore (On the Body), on materialist metaphysics and natural philosophy, De Homine (On Man), and De Cive (On the Citizen), progressing from bodies to humans to political society.

**English Civil War and exile**
Hobbes fled to Paris around 1640 as conflict between king and Parliament grew, and he wrote Leviathan in exile there, shaped by the chaos of the English Civil War. While in Paris he served as mathematics tutor to the future Charles II.

**Translation of Thucydides**
Hobbes published the first English translation directly from the Greek of Thucydides's History of the Peloponnesian War in 1629. He presented it partly as a warning about the dangers of democracy.

**Third Objections to Descartes**
Hobbes wrote the third set of objections published with Descartes's Meditations, arguing from a materialist standpoint against Descartes's claim that the mind is an immaterial substance.

**Born of fear: the Spanish Armada**
Hobbes was born prematurely in 1588 in Malmesbury, supposedly because his mother went into labor on hearing of the approaching Spanish Armada. He later quipped that "fear and I were born twins," and Leo Strauss argued that Hobbes made the fear of violent death the foundation of his moral and political philosophy.
